lessons.title: Objects, not text - why it matters
lessons.body:
PowerShell pipes OBJECTS with named fields, not lines of text. That makes it a query language over the whole machine - close to SQL, which your background makes intuitive:
  Get-Process | Where-Object CPU -gt 100 | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select Name,Id,CPU
reads as SELECT name,id,cpu FROM processes WHERE cpu>100 ORDER BY cpu DESC. Because it is built on .NET it can reach processes, services, the registry, event logs, the firewall, WMI/CIM, and Active Directory - and it is already on every Windows box, which is why both admins and attackers live in it.

lessons.title: Local enumeration cheat-set
lessons.body:
The first questions on any host - what is here, what runs, what listens:
  Get-Process                         running programs
  Get-Service | ? Status -eq Running  running services
  Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | select Name,StartName,PathName   service account + binary
  Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen  open local ports and owning PID
  Get-LocalUser ; Get-LocalGroupMember Administrators   who is local admin
  Get-ScheduledTask | ? State -ne Disabled             autostart via tasks
  Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\...\CurrentVersion\Run'      autostart via registry
For each result ask: what is this, and should it be here? That is threat hunting.

lessons.title: Enumerating the whole domain
lessons.body:
With RSAT's ActiveDirectory module (on a domain-joined box with rights) you can map an entire organization:
  Get-ADDomainController -Filter *        every domain controller (the crown jewels)
  Get-ADComputer -Filter * -Properties OperatingSystem | select Name,OperatingSystem
                                          every computer in the domain
  Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties LastLogonDate        every user account
  Get-ADGroupMember 'Domain Admins'       who holds the keys
This is exactly what an attacker runs after landing one credential - and what BloodHound collects automatically. DEFENSE: tiering, limiting who can read sensitive attributes, and alerting on bulk AD enumeration.

lessons.title: How permissions leak
lessons.body:
Most privilege escalation is a wrong answer to 'who can touch this?'. Common leaks:
  Get-Acl C:\path | Format-List       read an object's owner + ACL
  icacls C:\path                       quick ACL dump; look for (F)/(M) for Users/Everyone
Leaks to hunt:
  - a service whose BINARY or folder is writable by normal users (replace it -> runs as the service account, often SYSTEM)
  - an unquoted service path with spaces (C:\Program Files\... -> C:\Program.exe hijack)
  - over-broad shares/ACLs granting Everyone or Authenticated Users Modify
  - nested group membership: a user is admin somewhere via a group inside a group
  - dangerous privileges on your token (whoami /priv): SeImpersonate, SeBackup, SeDebug
Each is least-privilege violated. DEFENSE: correct ACLs, quoted paths, minimal group nesting, and removing privileges nobody needs.

lessons.title: Living off the land, and how it is caught
lessons.body:
Attackers prefer built-in PowerShell because it looks like admin work and drops no malware ('living off the land'). So defenders instrument it:
  - Script Block Logging records the actual code that ran (event ID 4104), even obfuscated
  - AMSI lets AV scan scripts in memory as they execute
  - Constrained Language Mode limits what untrusted scripts can do
  - Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security';Id=4625}   failed logons (brute force)
Knowing both sides - what the cmdlets can do and how they are logged - is the whole game.

quiz.q: What does PowerShell pass between pipeline stages?
quiz.why: Objects with properties - why it feels like querying the machine.
The ActiveDirectory module's Get-ADDomainController enumerates DCs.

quiz.q: A service whose binary is writable by normal users lets you...
options: run code as the service account (often SYSTEM)
quiz.why: Replace the binary; it runs with the service's privileges at next start.

quiz.q: Which event ID records failed logons (useful for spotting brute force)?
quiz.why: 4625 = failed logon. (4104 is script block logging.)

quiz.q: Why do attackers favor built-in PowerShell?
options: It drops no malware and looks like admin activity
quiz.why: 'Living off the land' blends in - though 4104/AMSI still catch much of it.
